intro/hello: Welcome to the case study, where everything from the last few chapters comes together.
intro/forty: Scores, the softmax loss, backpropagation, gradient descent: it all fits in about forty lines of NumPy, and we will write every one.
intro/data: The data is a toy: three hundred points in a flat plane, in three colors, wound into a spiral.
intro/why2d: Two dimensions are the point: with images we only get a loss curve, but in a plane we can see exactly what each model learned.
intro/lin: First, a softmax linear classifier. Its loss goes down, and it still gets only about half the points right.
intro/why: That failure is instructive: every edge it can draw is a straight line.
intro/net: Then a handful of changed lines add one hidden layer, and the same training gets almost every point right.
intro/loop: Both models learn with the same four-step loop: compute the scores, measure the loss, backpropagate the gradient, and step downhill.
intro/go: Let us start with the data.
data/shape: There are K equals three classes, with N equals one hundred points each, and every point is two numbers, so D equals two.
data/rows: So X has three hundred rows and two columns, and y holds each row's class: zero, one or two.
data/loop: Each class is one arm of the spiral, and a loop builds the arms one at a time.
data/polar: The recipe is polar coordinates: a distance from the center, and a direction.
data/r: The distance r grows evenly from zero to one, so each arm starts at the center and ends at the rim.
data/t: Meanwhile the angle t turns: arm j starts at four j radians and sweeps four more, a bit under two thirds of a turn.
data/noise: A little random noise jiggles every angle, so the arm comes out fuzzy.
data/xy: Sine and cosine turn each distance and angle into the two coordinates: r sine t, and r cosine t.
data/walk: Each arm is a walk outward while turning, each starting four radians after the last, so the three arms wind around each other.
data/lab: Every point in arm j gets the label j.
data/cut: Now try to separate the colors with a straight line. You cannot: any straight cut slices through all three arms.
data/pre: Real data is usually normalized first, but these points already lie between minus one and one.
scores/params: A linear classifier has weights W, a matrix with one row per input dimension and one column per class: two by three.
scores/init: We fill W with small random numbers, a hundredth of a standard bell curve, and the bias b with zeros.
scores/mult: The scores then come from one matrix multiply: each row of X, dotted with each column of W, gives one score per class.
scores/shapes: Check the shapes. Three hundred by two, times two by three, gives three hundred by three: three scores for every point.
scores/bcast: The bias is a single row of three numbers, and NumPy broadcasting stretches it down all three hundred rows.
scores/row: Follow one point. Row sixty sits at zero point three seven, minus zero point four eight, in class zero. Its three scores come out tiny, because the weights are tiny.
scores/ch4: This is chapter four's score function, with examples stored as rows, so it reads X times W.
scores/pred: The predicted class of a point is just the class with the highest score.
scores/wedges: Color every spot in the plane by its winning class, and you see what a linear classifier draws: three wedges with straight edges.
scores/planes: Each class score is a tilted flat plane over the map, and two flat planes meet along a straight line. Training can turn and shift those lines, never bend them.
loss/job: Next, one number for how badly the scores fit the labels: the softmax loss, also called cross entropy.
loss/trained: To see the steps, take three points, rows sixty, one sixty and two sixty, scored by a classifier that has trained a while.
loss/exp: Step one: exponentiate every score. Whatever a score was, positive or negative, e to that power is always positive.
loss/norm: Step two: divide each row by its own sum. Now every row is three positive numbers adding up to one: a probability for each class.
loss/pick: Step three: pick each row's probability for the correct class. Indexing with range and y grabs one entry per row.
loss/log: Then take minus its log: a probability of one costs nothing, and as the probability shrinks toward zero, the cost climbs without limit.
loss/avg: Average the costs over all three hundred points, and that is the data loss.
loss/reg: On top goes regularization: half of reg, the strength lambda, times the sum of all the squared weights. The half makes its gradient come out clean.
loss/start: Now a cheap sanity check. At the very start the weights are tiny, so every class gets about one third.
loss/log3: So every point costs minus the log of a third, which is the log of three, about one point zero nine nine. The first loss should be that number, and it is: one point zero nine six.
dscores/back: To improve, we need the gradient. Backpropagation starts at the loss and works backward, and its first stop is the scores.
dscores/formula: For the softmax loss, it is beautifully simple: for each class k, the probability p k, minus one if k is the correct class.
dscores/why1: Why so simple? Write the loss out. Minus the log of that fraction is minus the correct score, plus the log of the sum of all the exponentials.
dscores/why2: Now nudge score k. The first part moves only if k is the correct class, and then by minus one. The second part moves by e to the s k, over the sum, which is exactly p k.
dscores/code: In code: copy the probabilities, then subtract one at each row's correct class.
dscores/ex: Read it as advice. Say the probabilities are zero point two, zero point three and zero point five, and the middle class is the correct one.
dscores/res: The gradient is then zero point two, minus zero point seven, and zero point five.
dscores/pos: A positive entry says raising this score raises the loss, so the wrong classes get pushed down, harder the more probability they hold.
dscores/neg: The correct class gets a negative entry: raising its score lowers the loss, so it gets pulled up.
dscores/done: And a point classified correctly with full confidence has a row of zeros. It has nothing left to teach.
dscores/div: Last, divide by the number of examples, because the loss was an average over all of them.
backprop/carry: Now carry the gradient one step further back, from the scores into W and b.
backprop/rule: The scores were X times W, plus b. For a matrix multiply, chapter six gave the rule: the gradient on W is the input, transposed, times the gradient flowing back.
backprop/shapes: No need to memorize where the transpose goes: d W must be two by three, like W, and only X transposed, times d scores, comes out that shape.
backprop/votes: In words: every point casts a vote on how to change the weights, scaled by its own coordinates, and the votes add up.
backprop/db: The bias was added to every row, and gradients add where paths meet, so d b is the sum of d scores down the rows.
backprop/reg: Regularization adds its own piece: the derivative of half of reg times W squared is just reg times W.
backprop/upd: Finally, the update: move every parameter a small step against its gradient, because the gradient points uphill.
backprop/gd: That is plain gradient descent, from chapter five, using all three hundred points in every step, with a step size of one.
backprop/one: And that is one full iteration: scores, loss, gradient, update.
train-linear/wrap: Wrap those lines in a loop, run it two hundred times, and print the loss every ten iterations.
train-linear/first: The first loss is one point zero nine six, just as the sanity check predicted.
train-linear/falls: Then it falls, fast at first, while the colored wedges in the background swing around to chase the arms.
train-linear/flat: After about fifty iterations it levels off near zero point seven seven, and stays there.
train-linear/acc: Now measure the training accuracy: predict a class for every point, and count how many are right. About forty nine percent.
train-linear/guess: That beats the thirty three percent of random guessing, but not by much. The ringed points are the ones it gets wrong.
train-linear/why: The picture shows why: however its lines turn, a linear classifier only carves the plane into straight edged wedges.
train-linear/arms: The spiral arms wrap right through those wedges, so each wedge catches pieces of other arms, and more training cannot fix that.
train-linear/bend: To follow a curve, the boundary itself has to bend, and for that we need a hidden layer.
hidden/ch7: Chapter seven showed that one hidden layer lets the boundary bend into any shape. So let us add one, with a hundred units.
hidden/two: Now there are two sets of weights and biases: W carries the two inputs to a hundred hidden values, and W two carries those to the three class scores.
hidden/count: That is six hundred and three numbers to learn, instead of nine.
hidden/lin: The forward pass gains one line. First, a linear layer just like before: X times W, plus b, a hundred numbers per point.
hidden/relu: Then pass each of them through a ray-loo, which keeps a positive number as it is, and turns a negative one into zero.
hidden/unit: Watch one hidden unit over the whole plane. Along one straight line, its input is exactly zero.
hidden/ramp: On one side, the unit is off. On the other it switches on and grows steadily, like a ramp rising from a flat floor.
hidden/many: A hundred units make a hundred ramps, each with its own line, tilted and placed by its own weights.
hidden/sum: The second layer adds those ramps up, with different weights for each class. The sum has a crease along every line, so the scores, and the boundary, can bend.
hidden/same: Everything after the scores stays exactly the same: the softmax, the loss, even the gradient on the scores.
backprop-net/longer: Only the backward pass gets longer, because the gradient has one more layer to travel through.
backprop-net/ds: It starts at the scores, with d scores computed exactly as before.
backprop-net/dW2: The second layer is a matrix multiply, so its weight gradient follows the same rule as before, with the hidden layer playing the part of X.
backprop-net/dh: We also need the gradient flowing into the hidden layer itself: the other half of the matrix multiply rule, d scores times W two transposed.
backprop-net/shape: Three hundred by three, times three by one hundred: one gradient for every hidden value of every point.
backprop-net/slope: Next comes the ray-loo. Its slope is one wherever the unit was on, and zero wherever it was clipped to zero.
backprop-net/gate: So on the way back it is a gate: the gradient passes where the unit was active, and is wiped out elsewhere.
backprop-net/dW: The first layer is one more matrix multiply. X transposed, times d hidden, gives d W, and summing down the rows gives d b.
backprop-net/reg: Both weight matrices get their regularization gradient: reg, times the weights.
backprop-net/rules: Every line here is a rule from chapter six, applied one layer deeper.
train-net/run: Now train the network: the same step size of one, the same regularization, the same loop, ten thousand times.
train-net/first: The first loss is one point zero nine nine, the log of three again, because all the scores start out tiny.
train-net/early: At first the background looks much like the linear classifier's wedges. Then, within the first thousand iterations, the boundary starts to curl.
train-net/follow: By two or three thousand it winds along the arms, and the rest of the run only polishes it.
train-net/loss: The loss settles at about a quarter, zero point two four.
train-net/acc: And the training accuracy is ninety nine percent. Almost every point lands on the right side.
train-net/lines: Now draw each hidden unit's line, the place where its input is zero: all one hundred of them.
train-net/poly: Look closely: the boundary is pieced together from short straight segments of those lines, a polygon winding along each arm.
train-net/crease: Each ray-loo puts one crease into the scores, and a hundred creases are plenty to trace a spiral.
compare/side: Side by side: on the left, straight edged wedges, the best a linear classifier can do, right about half the time.
compare/right: On the right, the network's boundary follows every arm.
compare/fwd: In code, the difference is small: one extra line in the forward pass,
compare/bwd: and a few more in the backward pass, to carry the gradient one layer further.
compare/params: Nine parameters became six hundred and three, and two hundred iterations became ten thousand.
compare/result: The loss fell from zero point seven seven to zero point two four, and training accuracy rose from forty nine percent to ninety nine.
compare/caveat: One honest caveat: that is accuracy on the training points, and it says nothing yet about points the network has never seen.
compare/fresh: For that you need held out data, as in chapter three. Here, a fresh spiral with new noise also comes out ninety nine percent right, but only checking could tell you so.
compare/a1: Assignment one asks you to write exactly this network, with mini batches, a validation set and a learning rate schedule, and train it on see-far ten images.
outro/recap: So here is the whole chapter in one breath. A complete classifier is a short loop of four steps.
outro/s2: Turn them into probabilities, and measure the loss.
outro/s3: Backpropagate: the probabilities, minus one at the correct class, and from there the matrix multiply and ray-loo rules.
outro/s4: Then step the parameters downhill, and repeat.
outro/layer: One hidden layer, one line forward and a few lines backward, took training accuracy from forty nine percent to ninety nine.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter: step through one iteration line by line with the real arrays, and train both models live in your browser.
